title: D&D Miniature Size Chart — What Scale Are D&D Minis?
description: D&D miniatures are 28mm scale. Size chart: Tiny (12-14mm), Small (21-28mm), Medium (28mm), Large (56mm), Huge (112mm), Gargantuan (224mm+).
html:
What Scale Are D&D Minis?

D&D miniatures use 28mm scale. A standard Medium humanoid measures 28mm to eye level, based on a 160cm eye-level height (175cm total) at 1:56 ratio. This is the baseline for all D&D miniature sizes.

D&D Miniature Size Chart

D&D 5e uses six size categories. Each category has a height range and corresponding miniature size in millimeters:

  • Tiny (under 2.5ft / 0.76m): 12-14mm — cats, imps, sprites
  • Small (2.5-5ft / 0.76-1.5m): 21-28mm — halflings, goblins, dwarves
  • Medium (5-10ft / 1.5-3m): 28-56mm — humans, elves, orcs
  • Large (10-20ft / 3-6m): 56-112mm — ogres, horses, trolls
  • Huge (20-40ft / 6-12m): 112-224mm — hill giants, young dragons
  • Gargantuan (40ft+ / 12m+): 224mm+ — ancient dragons, tarrasque

How to Scale D&D Miniatures

To convert between D&D size categories, use these percentages in your slicer:

  • Small to Medium: 133% (21mm to 28mm)
  • Medium to Large: 200% (28mm to 56mm)
  • Medium to Huge: 400% (28mm to 112mm)
  • Medium to Gargantuan: 800% (28mm to 224mm)

Use uniform scaling across all axes. Enter the percentage in your slicer's scale settings.

Standard D&D Mini Size

The standard D&D mini size for a Medium humanoid is 28mm to eye level. This is the size you get from official Wizards of the Coast miniatures and most 28mm STL files. If your mini measures 28mm from base to eye level, it is correctly scaled for D&D.

FDM Printing Tips for D&D Miniatures

Use a 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layer height for humanoid faces. Print at 20-30mm/s for outer walls. Orient the face upward to minimize visible layer lines on the most important detail area.

title: Warhammer 40K Scale Guide — 32mm Primaris Miniatures
description: Complete guide to Warhammer 40k miniature scales, Primaris vs Firstborn differences, and scaling percentages for 3D printing.
html:
What Scale Is Warhammer 40k?

Warhammer 40k uses '32mm heroic' scale, but this label is misleading. Primaris Space Marines measure approximately 40mm to helmet top and 35mm to eye level. The '32mm' label comes from the community convention when Games Workshop transitioned from 28mm around 2014-2015.

Primaris vs Firstborn Scale

Firstborn Space Marines are closer to 28mm-30mm. Primaris are noticeably larger at 35mm eye-level. If you are mixing old and new kits, scale the Firstborn up to 114.3% to match Primaris proportions.

Converting TO and FROM 40k Scale

Converting 28mm to 32mm (40k): set slicer to 114.3%. Converting 32mm (40k) to 28mm: set slicer to 87.5%. These percentages use eye-level measurements for maximum accuracy.

FDM Tips for 40k Miniatures

0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layer height gives the best facial detail. For vehicles and terrain, 0.4mm nozzle at 0.2mm layers is fine. Resin is preferred for character models with fine detail.

title: STL Scale Conversion Chart — Full Printable Reference
description: Complete STL scale conversion chart covering all gaming and ratio scales. Print this reference for your workshop.
html:
Why You Need a Conversion Chart

When converting miniatures between scales, you need the exact percentage to enter in your slicer. This chart covers all common conversions between 28mm, 32mm, 35mm, 40mm, 75mm, 1:35, 1:48, 1:56, 1:72, and 1:100.

Gaming Scale Conversions

The most common conversions: 28mm to 32mm = 114.3%, 32mm to 28mm = 87.5%, 28mm to 35mm = 125.0%, 28mm to 40mm = 142.9%. These are based on eye-level measurements at a 175cm human baseline (160cm eye level).

Ratio Scale Conversions

Ratio scales use top-of-head measurements. 1:56 to 1:35 = 160.0%, 1:72 to 1:56 = 115.2%, 1:100 to 1:35 = 285.7%. These are standard scale model conversions used by military modelers.

How to Use This Chart

Find your source scale in the left column, your target scale in the top row, and read the intersection percentage. Enter that percentage in your slicer using uniform scaling across all axes.

title: Bolt Action Scale Guide — 28mm WWII Miniatures
description: Scale guide for Bolt Action 28mm WWII miniatures including infantry, vehicle scales, and 3D printing recommendations.
html:
Bolt Action Scale Overview

Bolt Action uses 28mm scale for infantry and 1:56 scale for vehicles. This combination provides realistic proportions on the tabletop. Infantry measure 28mm to eye level, and a Sherman tank at 1:56 is approximately 14cm long.

Vehicle Scale Compatibility

1:56 is the standard vehicle scale for Bolt Action. 1:48 vehicles work but are slightly oversized. 1:35 vehicles are too large for 28mm infantry but make excellent display pieces.

3D Printing for Bolt Action

FDM is ideal for Bolt Action because the 28mm scale and 1:56 vehicles fall in the sweet spot for FDM detail. Use 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layer height for infantry, and 0.4mm nozzle at 0.2mm for vehicles.

title: FDM Miniature Printing Guide — Settings and Techniques
description: Complete FDM printing guide for miniatures covering nozzle sizes, layer heights, orientations, and post-processing.
html:
FDM Settings for Miniatures

Use a 0.2mm nozzle for miniatures under 40mm. Layer height should be 0.06-0.08mm for faces and detail areas. Print speed should be 20-30mm/s for outer walls. Use tree supports for overhangs.

Orientation Matters

Print miniatures face-up whenever possible. This puts the most visible detail (face, chest) on the top surface where FDM has the best quality. Avoid printing faces against the build plate.

Post-Processing

Light sanding with 400-600 grit removes minor layer lines. A coat of filler primer (such as Tamiya Surface Primer) fills remaining lines before painting. Two thin coats of primer are better than one thick coat.

title: Converting Real-World Objects to 32mm Scale
description: Formula and reference chart for converting real-world measurements to 32mm miniature scale for terrain and scratch-building.
html:
The Formula

To convert any real-world measurement to 32mm scale: (inches × 25.4 / 72) × 32 = mm at 32mm scale. Simplified: inches × 11.29 = mm. For metric: cm × 1.829 = mm at 32mm scale.

Quick Reference

A 6-foot (183cm) human = 32mm. A standard door (6'8" / 203cm) = 35.7mm. A car (15ft / 457cm) = 203mm. A two-story house (20ft / 610cm) = 271mm.

Application for Terrain

When building scratch terrain, measure the real object, apply the formula, and cut materials to the calculated miniature size. This ensures buildings, walls, and accessories look proportional next to 32mm miniatures.

title: Upscaling 3D Prints — When Detail Reaches Its Limit
description: Understanding the detail limits when scaling up 3D printed miniatures, and when resin becomes necessary over FDM.
html:
Detail Limits by Scale

FDM produces acceptable detail up to approximately 75mm for most miniatures. Beyond 75mm, layer lines become visible on smooth surfaces even at 0.06mm layer height. Resin printers maintain detail to 150mm+ because their layer lines are typically 0.025-0.05mm.

The Math of Visible Layer Lines

At 0.06mm layer height, each layer step is visible on surfaces angled less than 45° from horizontal. As the model gets larger, these steps become proportionally more noticeable. At 75mm, a 0.06mm step represents only 0.08% of the total height — barely visible. At 32mm, the same step is 0.19% — still acceptable.

When to Switch to Resin

Switch to resin when: the model has fine chain, wire, or antenna detail; the model will be displayed at eye level in a cabinet; or the model exceeds 75mm and needs smooth curved surfaces.

title: 28mm to 32mm Percentage — The Complete Guide to 114.3%
description: Everything you need to know about the 114.3% conversion from 28mm to 32mm scale, including the math, slicer settings, and common use cases.
html:
The Short Answer

Set your slicer to 114.3% uniform scaling when converting 28mm miniatures to 32mm scale. This is the most common conversion in the tabletop hobby because it bridges D&D/PF (28mm) and Warhammer 40k/AoS (32mm).

The Math

32mm eye-level ÷ 28mm eye-level = 1.143 = 114.3%. The eye-level baseline is measured at 160cm on a 175cm human figure. This matches the community convention for gaming scales.

When to Use 114.3%

Use this percentage when: converting D&D miniatures to 40k scale, scaling Pathfinder models for Age of Sigmar, or enlarging any 28mm STL to match 32mm tabletop standards.

Resin Shrinkage Note

Standard resin shrinks 0.5-1%. If precision matters, use 115% instead of 114.3% to compensate. PLA shrinkage (0.8-2%) is usually canceled by typical FDM over-extrusion.

title: Why 175cm? The Human Baseline for Miniature Scale
description: Explanation of why 175cm is used as the standard human height reference for miniature scale measurements.
html:
The 175cm Standard

175cm (5'9") is the average adult male height used as the reference point for miniature scale calculations. At 1:56 ratio (28mm scale), a 175cm human becomes 31.25mm total height, or 28mm to the eye level at 160cm.

Why Not 180cm or 170cm?

175cm is the median across European and North American populations, which covers the majority of the miniature wargaming market. It also produces clean division results for common ratio scales: 1750mm ÷ 56 = 31.25mm, 1750mm ÷ 50 = 35mm, 1750mm ÷ 48 = 36.46mm.

Eye Level vs Total Height

The eye-level height (160cm) is used for gaming scales because miniatures are typically viewed from a slight downward angle at tabletop distance. The top-of-head height (175cm) is used for ratio scales because scale modelers measure total figure height.

title: How to Measure Miniature Scale — Eye Level vs Top of Head
description: Step-by-step guide to measuring your miniatures to determine their actual scale using calipers or ruler.
html:
What to Measure

Measure from the base of the miniature (top of the base, not bottom) to the eye level of the figure. For most humanoids, eye level is approximately 85-90% of total height. For armored figures with helmets, measure to the visor line.

Tools You Need

Digital calipers give the most accurate reading (0.01mm precision). A standard ruler works for quick checks. Most slicers have a built-in ruler tool that measures STL models in millimeters.

Interpreting Your Measurement

28mm eye-level = 28mm scale (D&D, Bolt Action). 32mm eye-level = 32mm scale (40k, AoS). 35mm eye-level = 35mm scale (Legion, MCP). If the total height is 30mm, the eye-level is approximately 26-27mm, which is closer to 25mm scale.

title: How to Scale STL Files in Chitubox & Lychee — Step-by-Step Guide
description: Learn how to scale STL files in Chitubox and Lychee Slicer. Step-by-step guide with exact percentages for 28mm, 32mm, and other miniature scales.
html:
Scaling in Chitubox

Open your STL file in Chitubox. Select the model, then click the Scale button in the left toolbar. Enter the percentage in the X, Y, and Z fields. Make sure Uniform Scaling is enabled so all axes scale together. For example, enter 114.3% to convert 28mm to 32mm.

Scaling in Lychee Slicer

Import your STL into Lychee. Select the model and open the Transform panel. Click the Scale tab and enter your percentage. Lychee shows the real-time dimensions as you type, so you can verify the resulting size before slicing.

Verifying the Result

After scaling, use the ruler tool in your slicer to measure the eye-level height of the figure. Compare this against the target scale: 28mm eye-level for 28mm scale, 32mm for 32mm scale, etc. If the measurement is within 0.5mm, the scaling is accurate.

Non-Uniform Scaling

Avoid non-uniform scaling unless you have a specific reason. Stretching a model on one axis distorts proportions and can cause fit issues with multi-part models. Always use uniform scaling for scale conversions.

title: Terrain Scale Compatibility — What Scale Terrain for Your Miniatures
description: Complete guide to matching terrain scales with miniature scales. Learn which terrain works with 28mm, 32mm, 35mm, and other gaming scales.
html:
Why Terrain Scale Matters

Getting terrain scale right is just as important as getting miniature scale right. A doorway that's too small for your minis breaks immersion. A building that's too large dwarfs your army. Terrain scale determines how your miniatures interact with the battlefield.

Terrain Scale by Miniature Scale

28mm miniatures (D&D, Bolt Action, Frostgrave): Use 1:56 terrain. Standard doorways should be 35-37mm tall. Walls should be 40-50mm tall. This matches the 28mm eye-level standard.

32mm miniatures (40k, AoS, Kill Team): Use 1:48 terrain. Standard doorways should be 40-45mm tall. Walls should be 50-60mm tall. Slightly larger than 28mm terrain to match the heroic proportions.

35mm miniatures (Legion, Conquest): Use 1:48 terrain. Standard doorways should be 45-50mm tall. Walls should be 55-65mm tall. Close to 1:48 scale model buildings.

40mm miniatures (Shatterpoint, MCP): Use 1:43 terrain. Standard doorways should be 50-55mm tall. Walls should be 60-70mm tall. Larger scale to match the character-focused gameplay.

Universal Terrain Rule

For any scale, the doorway rule works: a standard door (200cm real) should be taller than your miniatures' total height (top of head + base). If your 32mm minis fit through a 45mm doorway, the scale is correct.

3D Printing Terrain Tips

Print terrain at 0.2mm layer height with a 0.4mm nozzle for speed. Terrain doesn't need the same detail as minis. Use 15-20% infill for buildings to save weight and material. Orient walls vertically for best surface finish.

title: FDM Print Settings Per Scale — Layer Height, Nozzle, and Speed Guide
description: Optimal FDM print settings for every miniature scale from 6mm to 75mm. Layer height, nozzle size, speed, and infill recommendations.
html:
Why Print Settings Vary by Scale

Smaller miniatures need finer settings to capture detail. Larger miniatures can use coarser settings for speed. The wrong settings waste time or produce poor results. Match your settings to the scale for best results.

6mm-10mm Scale (Epic)

Nozzle: 0.2mm (required for detail). Layer height: 0.04-0.06mm. Speed: 15-20mm/s for outer walls. Infill: 20-30%. Notes: 6mm infantry is nearly impossible on FDM — use resin. 6mm-10mm vehicles and mechs are manageable with a 0.2mm nozzle.

15mm Scale (Historical)

Nozzle: 0.2mm recommended. Layer height: 0.06-0.08mm. Speed: 20-25mm/s for outer walls. Infill: 15-20%. Notes: 15mm infantry benefits from resin. Vehicles and terrain print well on FDM with a 0.2mm nozzle.

28mm Scale (D&D, Bolt Action)

Nozzle: 0.2mm for infantry, 0.4mm for terrain. Layer height: 0.06-0.08mm. Speed: 20-30mm/s for outer walls. Infill: 15-20%. Notes: The FDM sweet spot. 28mm miniatures print well with basic FDM settings. Resin gives cleaner facial detail.

32mm Scale (40k, AoS)

Nozzle: 0.2mm for infantry, 0.4mm for vehicles. Layer height: 0.06-0.08mm. Speed: 20-30mm/s for outer walls. Infill: 15-20%. Notes: 32mm is forgiving on FDM. Layer lines are less visible on larger surfaces. Heroic proportions hide imperfections.

35mm-40mm Scale (Legion, MCP)

Nozzle: 0.2mm for detail, 0.4mm for speed. Layer height: 0.06-0.08mm. Speed: 20-30mm/s for outer walls. Infill: 15-20%. Notes: Large enough for FDM to handle facial detail well. Use 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layer height for faces.

75mm Scale (Display)

Nozzle: 0.2mm required. Layer height: 0.04-0.06mm. Speed: 15-20mm/s for outer walls. Infill: 10-15%. Notes: 75mm on FDM needs very fine settings. Slow print speeds are essential for acceptable surface quality. Consider resin for the best results.
